title.narrative: UNESCO, Better Education Systems for Afghanistan’s future 2018-2025
UNESCO, Bättre utbildningssystem för Afghanistans framtid 2018-2025

description.narrative:
Syftet med insatsen är att bidra till rättvis tillgång till utbildning av hög kvalitet i Afghanistan 2018-2023. Unescokontoret i Kabul kommer att säkerställa genomförandet av programmet, inklusive samordning, expertstöd, uppföljning och utvärdering. Sveriges bidrag är 180 miljoner SEK.
Det övergripande målet med insatsen är att bidra till tillgång av utbildning av god kvalitet för den afghanska befolkningen, med ett särskilt fokus på flickor och kvinnor.

The purpose of the intervention is to contribute to equitable access to quality education in Afghanistan 2018-2023, through efficient and transparent management of the education sector. UNESCO Office in Kabul will ensure program implementation including coordination, technical support, monitoring and evaluation. The total Swedish support is 180 million SEK.
The overall goal is to contribute to increased access to education of good quality for the afghan people, with a specific focus on girls and women.

The purpose of the intervention was to contribute to access to quality education in Afghanistan.
It is relevant to note that the programme started under the previous government and was reprogrammed (see previous amendment from 13 July 2022, dox 026299/22) in 2022. The programme faced several limitations due to the political situation of the country, therefore, a large part of the presented results are at the output level. After the Taliban takeover, the support was provided off-budget, and without undue influence by the Taliban de facto authorities on the planning, implementation, and management of activities or beneficiary selection.
The objectives during the origianal phase - System Strengthening and Government Partnership (July 2018 - 15 August 2021):
Outcome 1: Ministry of Education has the capacity to develop robust education sector plans integrating a gender perspective, underpinned by accurate and reliable education sector data, and to support and monitor their implementation.
Outcome 2: Revised curricula and learning resources for formal basic education (grades 1-12), non-formal adult education (level 2), and curriculum standards for higher education (selected education-related priority areas) are developed and implemented.
Outcome 3: Access to and demand for adult education and literacy for marginalized and disadvantaged groups and communities are expanded.
The objectives during the reprogrammed and cost-exthension phase (July 2022 - December 2025):
Outcome 1: Monitoring education data integrating a gender perspective to ensure the right to education for all children and youth in Afghanistan.
Output 1.8: Completion of the analysis on the grade 3 Students Learning Assessment (SLA) and the finalization of the SLA report.
Outcome 2: Quality of education is enhanced through developing curriculum for non-formal adult education, teacher training support, higher education, and girls' education.
Output 2.8: Provision of distance and online learning scholarships to 240 female students residing in Afghanistan to enroll in distance and online learning higher education programmes in neighboring countries such as Pakistan, Iran, India, and Uzbekistan considering language similarities and cost-effectiveness.
Output 2.9: Design and implement no-tech, low-tech, and high-tech contextualized approaches to provide quality distance education opportunities for 2000 secondary school-aged girls including hybrid and Interactive Radio Instruction programme.
Outcome 3: Access to and demand for adult education and literacy for marginalized and disadvantaged groups and communities.
Output 3.1.1: Provision of Basic General Literacy for 6000 adult literacy learners (over 60% female).
Output 3.1.2: Provision of Skills Based Literacy for 2400 adult literacy learners (over 60% female).

During the implementation of the Better Education System for Afghanistans Future (BESAF) programme (20182025), significant results were delivered across its original, reprogrammed, and cost-extension phases, adapting to the radical shift in political and social context following August 2021.
Expected Achievements & Primary Key Results
- Youth & Adult Literacy: Enrolled and trained over 30 955 youth and adult learners in basic and skills-based literacy across multiple provinces. Women represented 67% of participants in Basic General Literacy (BGL) and 85% in Skills-Based Literacy (SBL).
- Curriculum & Instructional Materials: Completed the National Curriculum Framework and subject syllabi for six learning areas during the original phase. Later, fully finalized the non-formal Youth and Adult Literacy and Basic Education (YALBE) Level 2 curriculum package (equivalent to grades 46) and digitized YALBE Level 1 into 192 videos and audio files.
- Teacher Professional Development: Exceeded teacher training targets by capacity building 1,257 teachers and master trainers in blended pedagogy (610 teachers) and Social Emotional Learning (647 teachers).
- Community Structures: Established 785 Village Literacy Committees (VLCs) across 11 provinces to drive community-level mobilization, facilitate class protection, and support female enrollment.
- Advocacy & Public Reach: Launched the national Literacy for a Brighter Future campaign, broadcasting educational messages and public service announcements that reached an estimated 25 million people across 34 provinces.
- Evidence Generation: Published 13 comprehensive research studies, surveys, and assessments including TVET mappings, higher education rapid surveys, and the Grade 3 Student Learning Assessment to fill critical data gaps.
Alternative Pathways & Innovative Achievements
- Higher Education Scholarships: Supported 577 women to complete their university degrees online following bans on female campus attendance.
- Alternative Secondary Education: Delivered remote secondary education to 1 723 out-of-school girls across more than 30 provinces using online and low-bandwidth digital platforms.
- Radio-Based Education: Broadcast curriculum-aligned instruction (Our Home, Our Class) and educational drama series that reached nearly 1 million listeners, including over 156 000 direct learners (over 80% female) across four focal provinces.
- Women's Livelihoods & Entrepreneurship: Provided professional internships to 55 women university graduates and business start-up grants to 45 women entrepreneurs.
- Low-Tech Mobile Learning Pilots: Tested alternative delivery channels, such as WhatsApp-based instruction for 129 girls and online English/life skills courses for 208 women.
Partially Achieved or Unintended Results due to Context-Driven Challenges
- On-Budget & Government Systems Support: Direct capacity development for the Ministry of Education (MoE) and Ministry of Higher Education (MoHE), as well as planned on-budget transfers, were suspended or halted after August 2021 to maintain donor principles.
Original BGL Target Gaps: Initial BGL enrollment reached 47% of its initial 15,000-learner target prior to August 2021 due to early delays with the Implementation Partnership Agreement and COVID-19 disruptions.
- National Policy Endorsements: Strategic frameworks, such as the National Education Strategic Plan IV (NESP-IV) and formal endorsement of general education curriculum frameworks, were left unfinalized due to government restructuring and the subsequent power shift.
- Public Campaign Restrictions: While billboard campaigns were intended for all provinces, installation was denied or restricted in certain regions by de facto authorities, limiting physical billboard coverage to 29 provinces.
The educational support has yielded more wider immediate results than expected, including improved psychosocial well being, informal employment and indirect reached a larger target group. Some of the female participants of Skills Based Literacy and higher education described during a Sida visit in Kabul that they were depressed and some even suicidal after being banned to attend school after the Taliban take over. By participating in alternative education provided by UNESCO they regained their spirits and in some instances saved their lives. Students described the programme as a source of hope, purpose, and emotional stability after years of exclusion.
Most participants stated that they were already teaching younger girls from their neighborhood, which gave them an informal income and benefited an indirect target group.
Below are some quotes from participants and a father of one participant:
"Before this opportunity I was very depressed, to a point that I contemplated suicide. But when I was able to study again, I felt a sense of purpose and regained hope."
"Before, I felt lost and uncertain about my future. Now, I am diligently preparing for the university entrance exam, and I am confident that I can make a meaningful difference in my community."
A father from Kabul stated: "My daughter was a top student, and seeing her spirit crushed after the ban was heartbreaking for our family. This programme did more than just educate her. It brought back her smile. It gave her community."
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
